html:
On 25 March 1807 the Slave Trade Act became law, making it illegal for British ships and subjects to trade in enslaved Africans. Britain had been the largest slave-trading nation of the 1700s.

The ban followed twenty years of campaigning. Thomas Clarkson gathered evidence, William Wilberforce led the fight in Parliament, Quakers organised, and Black writers such as Olaudah Equiano told their own stories. Petitions and a boycott of slave-grown sugar spread the cause.

The act did not free anyone already enslaved; that came with the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. From 1808 the navy's West Africa Squadron hunted slave ships and landed the freed captives at Freetown. The United States banned imports in 1808. But the Atlantic slave trade went on illegally for decades, mostly to Brazil and Cuba, until the 1860s.
